# The Warranty Card

For thirty-one years I wrote instruction manuals for the Halvorsen Appliance Company, and in every one of them I hid a single sentence that did not belong.

Not a secret message, exactly. Nothing a lawyer would flag. Just one line that was a little softer than the others, tucked between the troubleshooting table and the warranty information, where no one reads anything at all.

In the manual for the Model 40 toaster, 1993: *If the toast is not the color you hoped for, adjust the dial and try again; most things improve with a second attempt.*

In the manual for the Aria countertop blender, 1998: *Allow the motor to rest between uses. Everything works better after it rests.*

In the manual for the Kestrel space heater, 2004, which went out to maybe forty thousand homes in the upper Midwest: *Do not leave the unit unattended. Do not leave yourself unattended, either.*

I started the habit the winter my husband left, when I was twenty-nine and writing, at that moment, a four-page guide to a hand mixer. I remember sitting at my desk in the Halvorsen building, the radiator clanking, reading the sentence *Always unplug the appliance before cleaning* and thinking that it was the most caring thing anyone had said to me in weeks. Someone had imagined me standing in my kitchen with wet hands. Someone had worried about me being hurt.

That was the job, I realized. Imagining strangers in their kitchens and wanting them to be safe. It was almost love, if you squinted.

So I added one more line. *Beaters may be washed by hand or in the top rack of the dishwasher. Take your time.*

My supervisor, a man named Gil who wore the same brown cardigan for the entire Clinton administration, read the draft and circled *Take your time* in red. In the margin he wrote: *Necessary?*

I wrote back: *Customers were rushing and bending the beaters.*

This was not true. But Gil nodded and let it through, and it went to the printer, and eighty thousand people received it folded in thirds inside a cardboard box, and almost none of them read it, and that was fine. That was the point, almost. It was like leaving a coin on a sidewalk. You don't need to see who finds it.

After that I did it every time. It became a discipline, the way some people pray before meals. I would finish the real work: the exploded diagrams, the parts lists, the careful passive voice (*The lid should be secured before operation*). Then I would sit for a while and think about who might be opening this box. A college kid with his first apartment. A widower learning to cook. A woman buying a space heater because the furnace died and the landlord wasn't answering. And I would write one sentence for them.

*The appliance may make a clicking noise as it cools. This is normal. You are also normal.*

That one Gil caught. We compromised on *This is normal and not a cause for concern.* I decided that was close enough. He knew what I meant, I think. Near the end, before he retired, he told me he'd started reading the manuals for his own appliances at home, looking for "the Halvorsen sentence." He'd never found one in another company's. "You're the only one doing it," he said, which I'd known, but it was nice to hear someone say.

---

I retired in March. The last manual I wrote was for a rice cooker, the Tamsin, a sleek white thing with a little screen that says *DONE* in a font I argued about for two weeks. My sentence for that one was *When the light turns green, the rice is ready; there is no need to check it more than once.* I was thinking of my own mother, who lifted pot lids compulsively, who never trusted that anything would turn out.

The company threw a small party. There was sheet cake. Someone gave me a framed copy of the Model 40 toaster manual, which was sweet, although I suspect it was chosen at random from the archive.

I thought that was the end of it.

Then, in June, a package came to my house, forwarded from the Halvorsen customer service department. Inside was a three-ring binder, the heavy-duty kind, with a handwritten label on the spine: *THE SENTENCES.*

Every page was a photocopy of one of my manuals, and on every page, one line was highlighted in yellow.

Not all of them. But a lot. Sixty-three, by my count. The toaster, the blender, the space heater. The hand mixer, *Take your time*, with the yellow ink gone slightly brown with age.

There was a letter tucked in the front pocket.

*Dear Writer,*

*I don't know your name. The company wouldn't tell me, which I understand.*

*My father ran a small appliance repair shop in Duluth from 1981 until he died last year. He kept the manuals for everything that came through. When I was cleaning out the shop, I found this binder under the register. He had been collecting these for almost thirty years. I didn't know. He never mentioned it.*

*He was not an easy man to talk to. He didn't say soft things. But I think he read these the way other people read horoscopes, or scripture. Some of them he'd underlined twice.*

*The last page is the one from a space heater. Next to "Do not leave yourself unattended, either," he wrote the date: February 2005. That was the winter after my mother died. I was in college and didn't come home much.*

*I don't really know why I'm sending this. I guess I wanted you to know that somebody found them.*

*Thank you for imagining us.*

It was signed only with a first name, and a line underneath it, in the same slanting hand:

*P.S. I bought the rice cooker. I only checked it once.*
